tldr: For humanoids lacking sufficient arm degrees of freedom, this paper generates a diverse distribution of 'when and how' to recruit the pelvis and waist anticipatorily using a CVAE, combining it with a reactive whole-body tracker to achieve high tracking success and zero-shot constraint adaptation.
hero_caption: Examples of diverse body recruitment strategies for the same bimanual task. When the body is fixed, 5-DoF arms alone lack the range of motion to reach the targets (left). However, multiple dynamically valid motions exist (right), such as lowering the pelvis, leaning forward, or twisting the waist.
overview:
Many humanoid robots emerging in recent years feature only 5 degrees of freedom (DoF) per arm. As a result, the arms alone cannot achieve arbitrary positions and orientations in 3D space ($SE(3)$). To perform bimanual tasks, "body recruitment"—coordinating trunk motion like the pelvis and waist—becomes indispensable. However, there is no single way to move the body to track end-effector trajectories. Countless multimodal solutions exist, such as leaning forward, twisting the waist, or dropping the center of mass. Moreover, the temporal choice of when to start moving the heavy trunk is critical. Conventional reactive whole-body controllers only scramble to move the body after the arms hit their joint limits (saturation), which causes delayed motion and frequent tracking failures.

To solve this, the authors proposed "AMBIT," a generative planner that previews the commanded future trajectory and proposes an entire set of dynamically valid, diverse body recruitment trajectories. First, physics simulations run offline to collect a wide variety of successful trajectory data, and a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) learns this conditional distribution. During online execution, the CVAE samples multiple candidate trajectories, and a non-learned verifier checks geometric constraints and dynamic balance to select the best one. A clever design choice is that rather than strictly enforcing the selected trajectory as-is, it is softly fed in as a posture reference to a whole-body differential-IK QP (quadratic program). This establishes an elegant division of labor: the learned model anticipatorily decides the coarse timing and direction of body recruitment, while the conventional reactive controller reliably handles fine millimetric residual errors at the end-effectors.

Evaluations in the physics simulator (MuJoCo) showed that AMBIT significantly outperformed conventional reactive trackers and deterministic regression models in success rate. Furthermore, it demonstrated the flexibility to adapt zero-shot to unseen constraints at training time—such as obstacles or wrist payloads—purely through online candidate selection.
contributions: Revealed through dataset analysis that dynamically valid body recruitment strategies for bimanual tracking on a 5-DoF arm humanoid form a diverse, continuous manifold with an intrinsic dimension of about 4.

Developed "AMBIT," a planner that integrates a CVAE conditioned on previewed future end-effector trajectories to generate diverse recruitment strategies, physical constraint filters, and a whole-body QP tracker.

Demonstrated zero-shot transfer across five types of constraint shifts absent during training (such as obstacles and wrist weights), maintaining high success rates purely through test-time sample selection without re-training.
Confirmed that zero-hyperparameter transfer to a different robot (Unitree G1) further widened the advantage over the tracker, and demonstrated kinematic realisability on a physical R1.

sections.heading: Can't Reach with Arms Alone? Recruit the Body with Anticipation and Diversity
sections.summary: Humanoids with 5-DoF arms cannot reach arbitrary end-effector poses with arms alone, making trunk recruitment essential, yet countless valid ways to move exist. While reactive controllers lag because they only move after arms saturate, this paper proposes a generative approach that previews future trajectories to select and execute from diverse strategies.
sections.details:
In humanoid manipulation, a low arm joint count is a severe issue. On recent physical platforms like the Unitree R1, each arm has only 5 DoF, making it impossible to freely control all 6 DoF (3 position, 3 orientation). Even combining both arms, reaching the 12-DoF bimanual task space requires adding two waist joints just to hit 12 DoF, frequently landing near singularities. Thus, recruiting the 6-DoF pelvis while maintaining double support is strictly necessary.

However, conventional reactive whole-body control (WBC) approaches—like running a prioritized QP where end-effector tracking takes top priority and remaining redundancy keeps an upright posture—have two pitfalls. First, "which body motion to choose" is not unique. Countless strategies satisfy the same end-effector trajectory, such as leaning forward, lowering the pelvis, or twisting the waist (Fig. F1). Second is "when to move." If the trunk only begins moving after the arms hit their limits, the heavy body cannot accelerate quickly enough, and end-effector tracking errors blow up.

In this work, the pelvis pose and waist trajectory over the entire task duration are defined as a "recruitment strategy $z$," which was found to form a diverse continuous manifold of dynamically valid solutions. The authors propose "AMBIT," a CVAE-based planner that previews commanded future end-effector trajectories to generate candidate strategies, achieving both tracking accuracy and early recruitment.

captions.F1: Comparison on an asymmetric lateral tracking task. Without trunk recruitment (left), the arms saturate at 0.82 s and end-effector error reaches 5 cm. In contrast, valid recruitment strategies moving the pelvis and waist (three examples on the right) accurately maintain the end-effector targets.

sections.heading: Moving from Per-Pose IK to Trajectory Generation Across Time and Dynamics
sections.summary: Conventional machine learning IK distributions remain static and pose-based, lacking temporal consistency and dynamics. This work considers entire valid body trajectories across the task, avoiding mode-averaging pitfalls in deterministic regression while integrating with existing whole-body QP trackers.
sections.details:
In robotics, probabilistically modeling the redundant solution space of inverse kinematics (IK) has been actively explored (such as IKFlow and IKDiffuser). However, these are fundamentally per-pose approaches that map a single target end-effector pose to a single joint posture. Applying this directly to time-series tasks causes severe chattering as control steps jump between different modes, breaking smooth motion and balance.

Meanwhile, conventional whole-body motion generation and controllers (such as momentum control or hierarchical prioritized task control) excel at finding and executing a single motion that satisfies physical constraints, but they do not explicitly preserve the underlying diverse solution space. Most recent reinforcement learning and imitation learning methods for humanoids also track a single reference motion.

AMBIT plays a complementary role to these approaches. It learns the conditional distribution of diverse, dynamically valid "temporally extended trajectories" and selects them online based on future constraints. Furthermore, it quantitatively demonstrates in dynamic tasks the known robotics pitfall of mode averaging: applying naive deterministic regression (e.g., MSE loss) to a multimodal distribution causes it to output an invalid mean solution sitting between modes.

sections.heading: Mathematically Formulating a Problem Solvable Only Through Body Recruitment
sections.summary: The problem is formulated as tracking bimanual $SE(3)$ trajectories over 3 to 6 seconds within a tolerance while feet remain fixed on the ground. Because arms alone saturate their range of motion in 99% of tasks with 5-DoF arms, a recruitment strategy leveraging the 6-DoF pelvis and waist redundancy is essential.
sections.details:
The target robot is the Unitree R1 (6 DoF per leg, 2 waist DoF [roll, yaw], 5 DoF per arm [3 shoulder, 1 elbow, 1 wrist roll], totaling 24 joints). The task is to track commanded bimanual end-effector (EE) trajectories $\tau_{EE}$ over 3 to 6 seconds in fixed double support. The end-effector tolerance $\varepsilon$ is evaluated at tight (2 cm / 10 deg) and loose (3 cm / 15 deg) thresholds.

Why is trunk recruitment indispensable? Evaluating 2,000 random configurations revealed that the 5-DoF single-arm Jacobian rank is strictly 5, unable to track a 6-DoF end-effector pose. Even combining 10 arm DoF and 2 waist DoF into a 12-DoF system, the median minimum singular value is $5 \times 10^{-3}$, dangerously close to singularity. If the body is fixed and tracking is attempted with arms alone, end-effector errors exceed tolerance and saturate in 99% of episodes.

Therefore, the sequence of pelvis poses and waist angles every 50 ms is defined as a recruitment strategy $z_{0:T}$. Leg joint angles are uniquely computed from pelvis poses via fixed-foot geometric constraints, while arms are solved by an end-effector tracking QP. In full-body simulation, the set of strategies where end-effector errors stay within tolerance, the center of mass remains in the support polygon, feet do not slip, and joint torque saturation stays below 5% of the duration is defined as the valid set $\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{valid}}$.

sections.heading: Inside AMBIT: Data Generation, CVAE, Selection, and Whole-Body QP Tracking
sections.summary: Diverse recruitment strategies are collected from an oracle and modeled with a trajectory-preview CVAE. At runtime, sampled candidates are filtered by geometric constraints and short-horizon QP verification, and the chosen strategy is softly fed to a whole-body differential-IK QP as a posture reference.
sections.details:
The AMBIT pipeline consists of offline data creation/training and an online selection/execution loop.

### IV-A Oracle and Dataset Construction
First, 3,000 episodes are generated across five task families, such as forward reaching and asymmetric lateral motions. For each episode, 41 candidate trajectories varying weights and onset timings are generated with a whole-body QP and evaluated in dynamic simulation. After deduplication, episodes with solutions contained an average of over 11 valid strategies. Key physical insights emerged: planned pelvis speeds above ~0.2 m/s caused rapid dynamic balance failures, and strategies that started moving the body gently more than 0.3 s before arm saturation had significantly higher success rates (60% vs. 46%).

### IV-B Generative Model (CVAE)
Strategy trajectories (8-DoF pelvis and waist deviations) are compressed to 128 dimensions via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). Future end-effector target trajectories are also compressed to 192 dimensions via DCT as condition vectors, training a 16-dimensional latent CVAE. A min-over-5 reconstruction loss over 5 samples is used to prevent posterior collapse where latent variables are ignored.

### IV-C Non-Learned Selector and Verification
At runtime, $K=16$ candidates are sampled from the CVAE in parallel. First, geometric constraints like obstacle keep-out zones are checked. Surviving candidates are ranked by an analytic cost function of end-effector error and smoothness, and top candidates undergo fast dynamic verification via a 1-second arm-only QP simulation. The first strategy to pass is committed.

### IV-D Execution Loop and Soft Reference Injection
The planner replans at a 0.5 s period. Crucially, rather than rigidly forcing pelvis positions (hard execution), the committed strategy is fed into a whole-body differential-IK QP as a posture tracking reference (soft execution). End-effector tracking weights (30 and 10) are set far higher than strategy tracking weights (5 and 1). Thus, the planner guides coarse body motion, while the QP makes real-time millimetric adjustments to end-effector residuals.

### IV-E Execution Layer and Torque Control
QP outputs are tracked by a 100 Hz floating-base inverse dynamics whole-body torque control QP. Without this torque control layer, simple joint PD control causes the robot to tip over immediately when moving its body.

sections.heading: Thorough Evaluation: Multimodality, Anticipation, and Zero-Shot Constraint Adaptation
sections.summary: In MuJoCo simulations, while deterministic regression collapsed from mode averaging, CVAE-based AMBIT achieved high tracking success. It adapted to unseen constraints like wrist payloads via online selection alone, and confirmed its efficacy on a second robot (Unitree G1) and hardware experiments.
sections.details:
All experiments were strictly conducted on held-out validation episodes where the oracle found a valid strategy (excluding inherently impossible tasks).

### V-A & V-B Multimodality and Mode Averaging (H1, H2)
The intrinsic dimension of the valid strategy set was approximately 4.3, forming a diverse continuous manifold rather than a few discrete modes. Training a naive deterministic regressor (B2) on this data yielded valid strategies only 35% of the time, failing physically because it averaged between modes. In contrast, the CVAE achieved 52% on a single sample and 82% when taking the best of 16 samples, demonstrating the clear superiority of multimodal generation.

### V-C Closed-Loop Success and Anticipatory Recruitment (H3)
In closed-loop tracking across 160 episodes, AMBIT reached 85% success at loose tolerance (3 cm / 15 deg) and 74% at tight tolerance (2 cm / 10 deg), significantly outperforming the reactive tracker (B1: 74% and 51%). AMBIT recruited the body before arm saturation in 48% of episodes compared to 35% for B1. Although the advance time difference appears small (tens of milliseconds), with pelvis speeds restricted to 0.15 m/s, this slight anticipation is decisive in preventing end-effector error blowups.

### V-D Zero-Shot Transfer to Unseen Constraints (H4)
Five constraints completely absent during training were imposed: pelvis height limits (ceiling obstacles), forward keep-out zones, waist range-of-motion limits, no-forward-lean constraints, and 0.75 kg weights on each wrist. AMBIT handled them purely through candidate filtering and CoM verification, outperforming the reactive baseline across all shifts. It also matched or exceeded a heavy test-time trajectory re-optimization baseline (B4) while being about 17x faster (1.5 s vs. 25 s).

### V-E Second Robot: Unitree G1
The exact framework was applied to the Unitree G1—which differs in morphology and mass (35.1 kg, 0.41 m arm reach)—without altering hyperparameters. Because the G1 is heavier, moving only after arm saturation is far too late. Consequently, reactive tracker success plummeted to 53%, while AMBIT maintained 85%, widening the margin to 32 percentage points.

### V-F Real-World R1 Validation
On a physical R1 suspended by an external support, generated recruitment strategies were executed. For commanded peak pelvis excursions (4.0 cm, 5.4 cm, 3.0 cm), the physical robot produced distinct motions of 3.5 cm, 4.7 cm, and 2.7 cm, respectively, tracking planned end-effector motion with a median error of 10.6 mm via encoder forward kinematics. While upright dynamic balance remains future work, kinematic realisability within the hardware's operational envelope was confirmed.

captions.F6: Tracking behavior on R1 (left) and G1 (right). With the body fixed, hands cannot reach the target spheres and drift significantly. In contrast, the body recruitment strategy derived by Oracle/AMBIT lowers the pelvis appropriately, tracking bimanual targets with millimeter-level precision.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work: Towards Real-Time and Free-Standing Physical Control
sections.summary: Body recruitment in humanoid bimanual tracking is a temporal decision-making problem with diverse solutions. AMBIT demonstrated strong tracking and constraint adaptation by blending a generative model with a whole-body QP tracker, leaving planning latency reduction and free-standing balance integration for future work.
sections.details:
In conclusion, for bimanual tracking on humanoids with low-DoF arms, how to recruit the trunk is the core bottleneck, and its solution space is multimodal. AMBIT demonstrated high tracking performance and flexible constraint adaptation by fusing a CVAE that performs anticipatory generation, a selector enforcing physical constraints, and a whole-body QP tracker correcting residual end-effector errors.

However, the authors candidly note several limitations. First, planner compute time in the Python implementation (~1.5 s) exceeds the 0.5 s replanning period, requiring simulation time to pause during planning for evaluation (though replanning at 1.5 s still comfortably outperformed baselines). Second, it assumes fixed double support without stepping for balance recovery or base relocation. Third, hardware validation was limited to externally supported kinematic execution; full free-standing balance via torque QP on hardware was not achieved due to control loop latency (up to 38 ms). These represent vital research challenges toward practical deployment.

takeaways: In bimanual tracking on low-DoF (5-DoF) arm humanoids, diverse solutions (intrinsic dimension ~4) exist for the timing and trajectory of trunk recruitment; naive regression fails due to mode averaging.
Because the trunk cannot accelerate abruptly (safe pelvis speed is under 0.2 m/s), anticipatorily and gently initiating body motion before arm range saturates is dynamically decisive for success.
Instead of rigidly forcing generative model outputs, softly injecting them as posture references into a downstream whole-body differential-IK QP achieves both high tracking accuracy and robustness.
Preserving a diverse trajectory distribution allows zero-shot adaptation to unseen geometric constraints and payloads purely through test-time non-learned filtering.
limitations: Planner compute time in Python takes about 1.5 seconds, leaving a gap for real-time closed-loop execution at 0.5-second periods without parallelization and speedups.
It assumes fixed double support and does not support stepping motions to expand reach or recover balance.
Physical hardware validation was restricted to kinematic tracking under an external support; achieving fully free-standing dynamic torque-controlled balance on hardware remains unresolved.
